children.text: The first decision was the name. Anything tied to the Day of the Dead or a national holiday would keep the brand inside the costume. The verbal identity had to carry courage, daring and pride, so the name became Alma Brava, brave soul: the part of you that fights for what it wants without fear of the limits along the way.

The identity is black, almost nothing else, with a typeface of generous proportions and a seal. It is elegant and fine, so the daring lives in the name and the restraint lives in the object. The brand book carries the line that sums it up: "Sentimiento icónico, orgullo de nuestra tierra."

The naming and the verbal identity. A logotype, a monogram and a seal. The brand book. The front and back label and the art direction for the bottle, and a product photoshoot. We made it between 2020 and 2021, with José Pablo as art director and Andrés Domínguez as creative director.
The Dieline and Packaging of the World both selected the work in 2021. The name was registered as a trademark the following year.

The name was still being tested when we started, and in production the gummy itself turned a dark red, between raspberry and red wine. We chose to keep the brand free of the product's color. José Pablo put it to the founders directly: "I don't believe that the brand must be aligned to the gummy color." Crimson stayed in the palette as an accent beside cobalt and mint.

The wordmark is heavy and rounded, black on cream. The pouch explains the product in plain steps, starting with taking Ando before you drink, and leads with a promise you can say out loud: less flush, more fun. Billboards and ads carry the same voice, built around the joy of going out without the flush.

Visual identity, color, the packaging dieline, home and product page designs in Figma, and a brand book. In 2024, revised labels and a travel tin, which Peter briefed as "Fun/playful/joyful, like everything that comes from our brand."

On the home page design, Peter wrote: "Ray and I LOVE this design! I think your team did an amazing job." Ando is on sale today at andogummy.com, and new clients have come to Atla since after seeing the project.

The product is a complete herbal system in phases, clear and then nourish, priced above the shelf. The problem was translation. The site had to teach what the products do so that anyone could follow it. Fernando's words: "Dumb it down." It also had to avoid looking cheap or pushy. Buyers of wellness, the strategy found, are tired of being sold to and tired of fake wellness.

The character we gave the brand is a health strategist: confident, direct and calm, a man who has seen both sides. The line that carried was your body isn't broken, it's blocked. Fernando picked the quietest of our moodboards, with the type and imagery of another. The logo is Magalie, softened and customized. Gradients follow the sky from sunrise to sunset, one for each product, the change a body goes through on its way back.

A moodboard and a strategy deck. Audience validation with personas. The graphic path: logo, a palette in purple, blue and orange, Playfair Display with ITC Avant Garde Gothic, jar boxes, social templates, a tote, cards and the website hero. Brand guidelines. Packaging for capsules, electrolytes and loose-leaf tea, with labels and box dielines. Event pieces: a banner, a hat, a booth and business cards.

Fernando, at the graphic path presentation: "honestly, I'm impressed right now. I have a smile that I can't hold back." Later, in writing: "I decided to give you all full reins on the rebrand." On the tea packs: "The doypack for the teas look fantastic." His site now opens with the strategy line: "Your body isn't broken. It's backed up."

The brief put the whole problem in one sentence: "We're human in a space dominated by robotic AI branding." The team wanted to feel premium: powerful first, then beautiful, then intuitive, and free of the glow and gradients the category leans on. In the middle of the project they chose a new name for the product, Anything, and the identity had to carry it.

The first route had a symbol. The client saw a news network in it, so we dropped symbols altogether. The brand became typographic: an editorial serif italic set against a plain grotesk, so the wordmark itself shows an idea turning into a product. A second mark, overlapping shapes tilted upward, became the icon the team calls the rocket. Photography went soft and dreamlike, with a computer standing alone in a field.

The logo and symbol. A palette of light blue and deep navy with pink and cream. A type hierarchy, icons, photography directions, the homepage with its "i want to build a..." prompt, social templates, launch assets, and a brand book in PDF and Figma. Later, animations for the logo, the symbol and the icons.

Zaria Zinn, founding designer, the day after launch: "our launch was yesterday and it went very well!! Thank you all so so much for your help getting us ready for it! Also wanted to say the computer in a field image has been a huge hit! Everyone can't stop talking about it!" The funding round that followed made TechCrunch.

Arc Studio was designed as a space for quiet luxury. A wellness environment where movement, recovery, and community flow together.

We translated that philosophy into a minimal identity built around the body in motion. A custom wordmark anchors the brand, while the symbol system abstracts the human figure and the letter A to represent Arc’s core experiences: movement, recovery, and shared flow.

Gradients draw from the heat of hot pilates, bringing energy and calm into the visual system.

An identity that moves with the body
and breathes with the space.

We showed them a rustic route with a community feel and another that mixed health science with luxury. Colson picked the rustic one and moved it east: rolling pastures, flowers, denim, red barns, embroidery, bottled milk and cows, "more 'east-coast farm' vibe as opposed to the more western vibe." Shannon fixed the words on the seal herself, Nature's Gold on top and Made in the USA below.

The wordmark is a cursive script drawn by hand, set in a roundel with a cow etched in a vintage line. The palette is soft: cream, sky blue, blush pink and a deep brown. Neutra Text and Nautica carry the type. The photography brief asks for love of the homeland and of the animals, and the pouches are shown in open pasture.

Vibe boards and moodboards, the logo and the brand guidelines, and labels for both products, taken through the manufacturer's compliance review. Then the website, which grew from a landing page into a full Shopify store with bundles and a page on why Bovi.

The manufacturer's quality lead wrote that the labels gave him "a farmhouse chic vibe that I think will do very well with consumers." At handover in May 2025, Shannon wrote: "It all looks great... We are very excited about how this turned out."

The founders, industrial designers in San Pedro Garza García, were turning a white warehouse into a place for children and families: art workshops, free play, a library, a shop and a café under one roof. They had a working name, The Lab, and one firm belief: art is a process, not a result. They needed a name and a brand before the space existed.

The hard part was the market, not the logo. Families there are used to structured entertainment and immediate results. The founders wanted to teach the value of free play and of paint on the floor, "where every stain of paint is a win." The identity also had to hold both audiences in one room: children at the tables and parents with a good coffee.

We showed directions: Playful Curiosity, geometric shapes that become characters, and Wholesome Imagination, storybook illustration. Laura Díaz de León chose the first: easy to keep in your head. The name came after the direction: Casa Colora, the house of color. A logotype a little disorganized and still balanced, a house-shaped seal, and stickers of clouds, hearts, hands and houses, drawn fat, like clay or shapes cut by small hands. Brown for the type, so beige and stickers never read as babyish.

Naming. Logotype in vertical and horizontal versions, the house seal, a palette of Soft Cream, Vivid Clay, Electric Azure, Dusty Rose, Sky Breeze and Muted Sage, Dunbar Tall with Galano Grotesque, the sticker graphics, photography direction, signage, cups, cards, a calendar and an Instagram system, all in a brand book.

The brief came down to a balance. The firm wanted to be seen as powerful and respected, and also as close and trustworthy. The monogram answers it by joining the C of Castro and the C of Capital with a plus sign, for what the firm adds to its projects and its investors. Around it, a modern and minimal system on a geometric grid, where the R and the P of the wordmark step forward.

Navy and royal blue carry the weight, with orange and cream for warmth, on a brand book, letterhead, email signatures, business cards and social templates. The posters speak to investors in plain Spanish: high-impact development, with transparent and concrete plans for where the money goes. The final files went out at the end of 2021.
Mindsparkle Mag published the work in March 2022. Through the following year, we sent it to prospective clients as a sample of our work.

Hanks has made full-grain leather belts in Endicott, New York since 1949. Made in the USA, with a guarantee measured in generations. The business sells online only, most of it on a phone. Almost every customer was a man. The company wanted to be known for women's accessories too, and the old identity, an uppercase HANKS inside a Circle-H, had nothing to say to them.

Mia Calleo, who runs Hanks, asked for a light touch: keep the name written out, change the font, keep the H. The question underneath was harder. How does a brand built for one audience make room for another without losing the first? Our first round leaned western and the client said so: too much cowboy, not enough accessory. Men's and women's goods needed one house with a door for each.

We kept the structure of the wordmark and reset it in a serif, Proxima Sera, with a monogram H marked EST 1949. The work that mattered was the palette. A saddle-brown core for everything Hanks, then secondary families: Tanned Oak and Raw Umber for men's pieces, Forged Teal and Washed Patina for women's. Photography moved away from the ranch. The client fixed the tagline herself: crafted in America, not just designed here.

Brand guidelines: tone of voice, mission, values, the logo system, color, type, photography and social templates. A logo package in every colorway. Website design in Figma for home, category and product pages, phone first, handed to their in-house developer to build.

Mia asked for the book to feel warmer and more welcoming than "male centric", and it was revised at once. Zach Duncan, the marketing partner who brought Hanks to us, said it plainly: "the brand redesign, I'm very happy with that on the hanks. You guys did a good job."

The strategy came first. The brand idea was "Con pasión, conexión", with adrenaline, trust and a wide range of activities as its flags. The mission was to make incredible experiences easy through a platform people can rely on. The vision went further: a platform that makes people fall in love with the planet and want to look after it.

The identity is warm and friendly. A yellow-orange serif wordmark sits on forest green, with coral and cream beside it, and a family of smiling mountains and hearts works as mascots on stickers and paper. The tone follows the personality written into the strategy: professional, adventurous, friendly and passionate.

A strategy deck, a moodboard, the graphic master and the identity presentation, then the final brand files at the end of 2021. Letterhead, envelopes, cards, stickers and a T-shirt for the guides, with the brand idea printed on the back.

The posters carry the line the brand was built on: strengthen your connection with nature, near the waves. Under it sat the values the client chose, connection with nature, fullness, community and a way of life. We kept the wordmark calm, a deep teal serif with a macron over the last A, and let the warmth come from drawings in thin orange line: palms, faces, people holding hands.

The logotype and its variants. Posters with the coastline coordinates, sunset photography and line illustrations. Envelopes, folders and business cards in deep teal, cream and burnt orange. Backlit signage for the entrance, shown in renders on a thatched gate. In 2023, animations of the mark and a looping beach scene.

In 2025 a prospective client wrote to us and named Mundã as the reference for her own brand. What she liked, in her words, was the simplicity of the brand, the people in it and its color palette, which she called interesting.

The identity is a thin, wide serif wordmark on a white can, with black and a cool cyan. The label works in English and in Arabic. It carries the product's claim, unique oxygenated water, the line Power for your life, a heart drawn from the water and oxygen formulas, and small icons for when to drink it: driving, flying, at the gym, at work.
A branding presentation, the logo and the can label. We used the work as one of our sales cases through the following year, and the water is still produced in Prague today.

Alex Bahram wrote the brief. He wanted a mix of serif and sans serif, a strong name and a strong logo that did not clash, colors that felt soft and welcoming without leaning feminine, and illustration alongside lifestyle photography. The team chose the first moodboard and then the first logo, and Lex Oiler wrote back: "We really love the logotype (simple! clean!) and love the heart."

The heart is the icon. It is made of pills that meet, and the break between the lines is what makes it read. Lex noticed it would animate well out of the P of Pathize. Cooper Light sets the titles and Circular the text, on cream, sky blue, mint and mustard. Hand-drawn illustrations and scribbles mark the words that matter, the way a person marks up a document.

Moodboards, the logo, a palette, illustrations and scribbles, a brand book, and applications: business cards, letterhead, the app icon, a pacing screen and pages for the website. The team asked for the raw files and the brand book in a hurry, to finish the relaunch. When it was done, Lex wrote: "We loved working with you guys."

In our reading, specialty coffee is crowded and much of it looks alike. The challenge was an identity bold enough to stand out on a shelf and still true to the café culture that started the company, carried from Turkey and Andalusia to Texas. It also had to work as a system, because new locations kept opening.

The mark is a tree: deep roots, growth outward. Apercu Mono sets the type, in warm earth tones with brighter accents. The company lives by its values, each a pair of P and B words: Prosper & Bond, Persevere & Become, Pause & Breathe, Patience & Belief, Pursue & Beckon. We turned each one into a linocut illustration, so the values travel on the bag instead of staying in a document.

The logo and its animation, an icon, iconography, a pattern and the type system. Packaging: the coffee bag, a box, labels and labels for the syrup bottles. The value illustrations, then applied across cups, totes, cans and shop windows.

The wordmark is a heavy serif, customized so every letter fits its neighbors while keeping its own bars and curves. To balance that weight, the icon is a smiling heart with a leaf on top, light and friendly, a little like a hairstyle. The team chose the bolder version of the logotype. Stickers carry the voice: for patients by patients, healthcare made easy, along for the ride with you.

The branding presentation, the logotype and the icon, a palette of peach, red, pink, light blue, yellow and cream, a set of stickers, and applications from posters and banners to envelopes and cards. The elements and assets went out in June 2022. That summer we also designed a quick-pay screen for the product, so patients could pay their providers faster.
Lex's verdict, written for us to share: "My only regret was not finding José and his team sooner. I'd recommend them to any of my friends." The following year he sent us Pathize Health.
Persona is a pioneer in personalized vitamins. More than five million people have trusted it with their daily routine, and its packs live on nightstands and kitchen counters in thousands of homes.

Persona's whole promise is that no two plans are alike. The challenge was making that promise visible at every touchpoint, from the box on the nightstand to the daily pack with your name on it, for a product people use every single day.

A rebrand built around one idea: only one you. A fingerprint mark, a dispenser box designed to sit beside the bed, and personalized daily packs that carry each customer's name. Five trillion combinations, one identity.

We started with the name. Gilad picked Puppy Py, after his own dog, Puppy Pie, whose spelling was already taken, and asked us: "If you can find a creative way around that it would be amazing!" The answer runs the name together in lowercase, stacked as pu ppy py, with a pPy monogram for the small places.

Color, illustration and photography carry the rest: bright yellow, red, orange, pink and lime, a dachshund wearing a rainbow holder, and a line that sums up the product, stand out from the pack. The moodboard, the branding presentation and the final files went out in June 2022. Gilad then redesigned the website himself on top of them.
He also introduced us to a friend who, in Gilad's words, "was very impressed with the work you did for me!"

His worry was obviousness. "Avoid anything too obvious or predictable. Simple and clear always works for me." Acre already had a brand and a whole family of things under it: a bar, the restaurant, weddings, treehouses. Rústico had to read as Acre's, the baby brother of a bigger restaurant to come, without competing with the reputation next door. A place like that cannot out-shout its setting. It has to disappear into it.

We showed several routes. Cam liked the burgundy in one; we recommended the structure of another with that color. He answered: "I trust you." The idea is a circle: seed, harvest, fire, table, community. A wordmark set in Forevs lifts the dinner from casual to ceremonial. A hand-led second logotype keeps the farm in it. Mulled wine, fired brick, terracotta and white linen: firelight in the field, soil underfoot.

Brand strategy and essence, the identity system and a brand book: primary and secondary logotypes, the "by Acre" lockup, color, Maison Neue with Caslon Ionic, a set of stamps, headline frames cut like flame, photography rules and social templates. Logo files and graphic elements, ready for the sign Cam needed right away.

Paolo Vincenti, co-owner: "We consider this approved." Rústico runs under the name, and Acre kept a page of its own for it because, in their words, it is new. The work grew into a brand manual for the whole resort, which the owners said they had been missing for some time.

The new identity is Y2K: a chrome wordmark on a pink ellipse over a blue and green gradient, airbrushed hibiscus, and an SLX monogram that works as a pill, a necklace and a gold hoop earring. The posters talk to the community directly, with lines like "Seen, supported, and celebrated" and "Guided from above, grounded from below."

María Martínez led the design. The brief, the branding presentation and the reviews ran through July 2022, and then weekly work on social graphics and the Shopify store until the end of the year. The posters describe the marketplace in Brittany's own terms: by us, for us.
That September, Brittany introduced us to Frank Bach, who was "extremely impressed with SLX's new branding", and described us to contacts at a16z as "the 360 agency that I've been working with."

Look at a tequila shelf and the blue is everywhere. His symbol, a rigid geometric knot in a circle, read like a keyboard key. And Carlos set conditions. His culture could never become a costume, and the story could not be about him: "hay que hacer mi historia en la historia de todos." Unido had to mean something you could say at a bar.

The idea was already in his brief: "unido is how you order it." Good tequila is offered and shared. We took the mariachi, his father's trade, as the cultural key without naming the family: a medallion label shaped by the sombrero, ornaments from the brooches of a mariachi jacket, a symbol that reads as rope, ribbon or bow. Paper, deep red, gold and green. The eagle was redrawn: the first one, in his words, was a pigeon.

A moodboard and the brand direction. Labels for Blanco, Reposado, Añejo and Extra Añejo, and the small bottle. Brand guidelines with the custom wordmark, symbol, badges, Schoolbook and Latino Gothic, photography direction and the Instagram system. A coming-soon page. The case box and the shipper art, ready to print for the distributor.

Carlos, on the first presentation: "sí me gusta mucho el concepto del sombrero del mariachi con el logo, siento que sí me entendieron." On the final white Blanco label: "I love it. I think that's the one." And: "I feel extremely blessed and happy to have you guys on board."

The mark is a round seal that stacks the letters A, T and B into one monogram, stamped in gold on cloth book spines of blue, coral, mustard and mint. Line drawings of hands at work carry the illustration. On the phone, the newsletter opens with the idea behind it: branding is a structural decision before it becomes a visual one.

Seal and wordmark, palette, illustration, the newsletter layout, and things to carry it: notebooks, a tote, a cap and cards. Readers sign up through Substack. Sponsors have written asking to advertise in it, and in November 2026 another studio shared it with its own community.

Rinske Fris styles male founders and executives, individually and online. Her clients are men whose businesses matured faster than their wardrobes. She had no logo, a website she barely used, and a styling app that accepts only a logo, a few colors and Google fonts. She found Atla through our content: "I feel like your messaging is so strong and I really like your feeling for design."

In her words, the service "solves the disconnect between how someone feels internally and how they show up visually." The market was the problem. Fast content, AI styling apps and generic influencers had filled the space with meaningless advice, so the depth in her work was hard to see. She wanted luxury, but "not Dubai-Loro Piana-luxury." Personal, a bit fun, calm. Her one word for the brand: alignment.

We drew moodboards: Structured Ease and Timeless Confidence. She chose the second. Quiet luxury that earns attention instead of demanding it. Refinement, not reinvention. Deep olive over ivory, with gold and brown. A stacked wordmark under the line Intentional Style, a monogram, a family of badges. Miller Display and Miller Text with League Spartan: the kind of serif she had pointed to in the moodboard.

Primary and secondary wordmarks, monogram and favicon, palette, typography, badge families, photography guidelines, an Instagram profile, post and story system, a brand guidelines book, and a newsletter template built in Flodesk.
Rinske, seeing the old and the new side by side: "now I'm like, what was I doing?" The next morning: "Very happy with the brand direction." Her newsletters have carried the olive wordmark since.

The restaurant is casual on a Tuesday, with ramen and sake, and formal on a Saturday, with author plates, and it needed a brand that could be both. The name already repeats itself. The identity had to turn that repetition into a character, so the place would read as one restaurant across both moods.

The wordmark mixes a casual type style with a formal one, so the name moves. The icon is a double-headed tiger sharing one eye, the duality and the repetition taken straight from the name. A kanji mark, 虎虎, covers the small places. Stickers carry the voice for everything else, with lines like "Sake it off" and "Have a rice day."

The logotype and its variants, the double-headed tiger, the kanji mark, color and type. Stationery and cards, stickers and labels, the menu, posters and flyers, a bag and packaging mockup, social templates and the design of the first website.
The restaurant is open, with a new menu for 2026.

The hard part, as we wrote in our notes at the time, was working inside identities that already existed, starting with the architecture itself. So the logotype is purely typographic, set in capitals, TORRE in a light weight and AVANCER in bold. The icon is a set of vertical lines taken from the architect's own sketches of the tower. The aim was a brand quiet enough to point at the building's details without covering them.

The logotype and the icon. A signage system drawn for the building: the entrance totem, the lobby directory with its restaurant and bar, pictograms, and a logo plate cut from metal. Stationery, folders and posters in dusty pink, terracotta and rust, with the sketch of the tower printed in ink. Social media for the tower and its tenants from 2021 to 2023.

We made it in 2022, working with Elipsis Arquitectos. Signage was a service the studio had never offered before. It started with this building, drawn so the signs would read as part of the structure rather than additions to it.

Persona Nutrition has sold personalized vitamin packs for years to an older customer, in a clinical, evidence-first voice. Jason Brown, its co-founder and CEO, wanted a second brand for younger women: non-medical, fun, built around wellness. There was no name he liked, an internal team already drawing looks, and a launch date set for the end of the year. He wanted an outside eye.

The problem was a brand that had never spoken to this customer. Persona's language was cold on purpose. The new one had to sound like a friend who knows her supplements and never makes you feel behind. And it could not look like a pill. Vyv sells daily packs, personalized, morning and night. Every image had to say pack, not capsule.

Jason sent a shortlist. We ranked Vyv first: short, modern, a real brand, with room to grow past vitamins. Of the directions we showed, he chose the one we called supplements that embrace you: sunset colors, curves, a happy brand. The logo is lowercase vyv built from a repeated triangle. Read it again and a woman appears in the middle. Expansive radial gradients spread from the center, for vitality.

Naming input and moodboards. Logo, logotype and a 3D mark. Brand guidelines with photography rules and Instagram formats. The gradient system as editable files. Packaging: the shipping box and the large and small dispenser boxes, in lilac and maroon, print-ready. The onboarding questionnaire. The homepage, desktop and mobile, handed to their developers.

Jason, after the guidelines: "I think it's amazing, keeping it both feminine, but also a strong color palette. I love the way the logo has developed." And later: "complete different energy than I would've ever expected for this brand." Vyv launched in January 2026. The next project was Persona itself.
